maya.name: Maya
signals: followed several new classmates this week
gaming club once · lives on campus

steps.label: COLD OPEN
steps.title: I already made a prediction about you.
steps.lead: Before you answer anything, make a call: could the apps you use every day predict you surprisingly well, or would they get the important parts of you wrong?
choices: PROVE IT — an app could predict me pretty well
NO CHANCE — it would get important things about me wrong
steps.hero: YOUR PHONE HAS BEEN COLLECTING CLUES. TODAY, YOU BECOME THE ALGORITHM.
steps.instructorCue: Do not explain or resolve the vote. Let students see the room split, then say: Good. Today we're going to find out who's right. Keep this question unresolved so you can return to it near the end.

steps.label: RETRIEVE + PERSONALIZE
steps.title: What does your algorithm think you are?
steps.lead: If an app had to describe you using only the traces you leave behind, what is ONE piece of information it could use? Think: what you watch, skip, search, buy, follow, pause on, where you go, or when you are online.
steps.placeholder: One signal an app could use to predict me is…
steps.instructorCue: Give students a minute to respond. Spotlight contrasting examples. Group responses verbally into behavior, identity, social, context, and history. Ask: which signals feel harmless, and which start to feel creepy?

steps.label: TEACH
steps.title: AI is not magic. It is a system.
steps.lead: Use one five-part lens to explain how Spotify, TikTok, Netflix, shopping recommendations, campus apps, and many other AI systems work.
flow:
MODEL / TOOL
patterns learned from examples

HUMAN INTERPRETATION
trust · ignore · question · misunderstand

DECISION / ACTION
click · buy · watch · share · go
steps.instructorCue: Teach one box at a time. Emphasize that pattern is not the same as understanding. Use a simple example: people who watched A + B + C often watched D. Then connect the output to a visible recommendation like 87% match or For You.

steps.label: BUILD THE ALGORITHM
steps.title: You are now the algorithm.
steps.lead: Build VIKING FEED, a fictional system that recommends one thing for Maya to do tonight. Decide what evidence matters, what patterns you would use, and what the system should recommend.
fields: MODEL / TOOL — What patterns should it use?
HUMAN INTERPRETATION — How should Maya read it?
DECISION / ACTION — What could Maya do next?
steps.instructorCue: Show Maya's profile and the four possibilities: Live Music Night, Gaming Tournament, Late-Night Pizza Social, Sunset Yoga. Students work alone first, then compare with a neighbor. Ask pairs what they disagreed about and why.

steps.label: PREDICT
steps.title: What should Viking Feed recommend?
steps.lead: Based only on Maya’s current profile, make the recommendation. Commit before seeing what the rest of the class chose.
steps.instructorCue: Let the room vote silently. Lock responses once most students have committed. Build suspense before revealing. Ask students to notice that they are making assumptions from incomplete data.

steps.label: REVEAL + CHALLENGE
steps.title: The class has spoken.
steps.lead: Now inspect the recommendation system instead of arguing only about the winning answer.
steps.prompt: What assumptions are hiding behind our recommendations? Did attending gaming club once mean Maya loves gaming? Do two pizza orders mean she wants a pizza social? Does music taste predict what event she wants tonight?
steps.instructorCue: Reveal the distribution. Ask someone to defend the least popular choice. Then run the assumption test: separate what the data actually says from what students inferred. Land on the phrase: DATA is not the same as MEANING.

steps.label: UPDATE
steps.title: New information changes everything.
steps.lead: Three new pieces of context just arrived. Recalculate your recommendation.
updates: Gaming club happened because Maya's roommate asked her to go.
Maya has been looking for ways to meet people outside her residence hall.
Maya has a major exam at 8 AM tomorrow.
steps.instructorCue: Reveal the three updates one at a time verbally, pausing after each. Ask students to vote again without discussing first. Then use the live changed-minds metric. Emphasize that the model did not suddenly become more intelligent—the information available changed.

steps.label: BEFORE vs AFTER
steps.title: The information changed. So did the decision.
steps.lead: Compare the room’s first recommendation with the second. Watch how the room moved when context changed.
steps.hero: NEW DATA → NEW OUTPUT → NEW DECISION. The model did not become more intelligent. The information available to the decision changed.
steps.instructorCue: Use the changed-minds number and side-by-side distributions as the visual centerpiece. Connect the shift explicitly to data quality, context, model assumptions, output, interpretation, and consequences.

steps.label: FAILURE TEST
steps.title: Find the failure.
steps.lead: Viking Feed makes thousands of recommendations. Where could the greatest risk enter the system?
choices: DATA — missing, wrong, or biased information
MODEL / TOOL — bad patterns or wrong objective
steps.instructorCue: Treat this like a game-show question, then reveal the distribution. Explain that there may not be one correct answer. Responsible AI is a whole-system problem, not only a model problem.

steps.label: HUMAN RESPONSIBILITY
steps.title: AI recommends. Who is responsible?
steps.lead: Imagine Viking Feed flashes: 97% MATCH — Go to the Pizza Social. Complete the sentence below.
steps.placeholder: Even with AI support, a human still needs to…
steps.instructorCue: Spotlight two or three strong anonymous responses. Pull out ideas like question, verify, consider context, understand consequences, and know when the AI might be wrong.

steps.label: RETURN TO THE PREDICTION
steps.title: So… can AI predict you?
steps.lead: Think back to your first choice: PROVE IT or NO CHANCE. After building and breaking a recommendation system, what would you say now—and what changed your thinking?
steps.placeholder: At the start I thought… Now I think… because…
steps.closing: AI IS NOT MAGIC. It is data, patterns, outputs, people, and decisions.
steps.instructorCue: Explicitly return to the unresolved cold open. Ask whether anyone changed sides and invite one or two explanations. Close with DATA → MODEL / TOOL → OUTPUT → HUMAN INTERPRETATION → DECISION / ACTION, then: AI can support a decision. It does not remove responsibility.
